item.question: Each case below gives three facts about triangle ABC and a second triangle. Say whether the two triangles are congruent, name the rule if they are, and write the statement in the right order. Case (a): AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = DF. Case (b): AB = EF, angle A = angle E, AC = ED. Case (c): AB = DF, angle B = angle D = 90 degrees, AC = FE. Case (d): angle A = angle D, angle B = angle E, AC = DF. Case (e): AB = DF, angle B = angle F, AC = DE.
steps_tex: Case $(a)$: count first. Three sides and no angles, so the rule is side side side. A goes with $D$, $B$ with $E$ and $C$ with $F$, so triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$.

Case $(b)$: count first. Two sides and one angle. Sketch it: $AB$ and $AC$ both start at $A$, and the angle is at $A$, so it sits between them. In the other triangle, $EF$ and $ED$ both start at $E$, with the angle at $E$ between them. The rule is side angle side, and the statement is triangle $ABC$ congruent to triangle $EFD$.

Case $(c)$: there is a right angle, so check the right angle, hypotenuse, side rule. The right angles are at $B$ and $D$. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so it is $AC$ in one triangle and $FE$ in the other, and they are equal. A leg is equal too, $AB = DF$. The statement is triangle $ABC$ congruent to triangle $FDE$.

Case $(d)$: two angles and a side, and the side $AC$ is not between the two angles. The third angles are equal too, because the three angles of a triangle add up to $180$ degrees. The rule is angle angle side, and the statement is triangle $ABC$ congruent to triangle $DEF$.

Case $(e)$: two sides, $AB$ and $AC$, and the angle at $B$. Sketch it and ask whether $B$ is squeezed between $AB$ and $AC$. It is not, because $AB$ and $AC$ both start at $A$. So the angle is not between the two sides, and no rule guarantees that the triangles are twins.
item.answer_tex: $(a)$: Congruent, side side side: triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$. $(b)$: Congruent, side angle side: triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $EFD$. $(c)$: Congruent, right angle hypotenuse side: triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $FDE$. $(d)$: Congruent, angle angle side: triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$. $(e)$: Not guaranteed: the given angle at $B$ is not between $AB$ and $AC$, so it is the side side angle arrangement.
steps: Case (a): count first. Three sides and no angles, so the rule is side side side. A goes with D, B with E and C with F, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.

Case (b): count first. Two sides and one angle. Sketch it: AB and AC both start at A, and the angle is at A, so it sits between them. In the other triangle, EF and ED both start at E, with the angle at E between them. The rule is side angle side, and the statement is triangle ABC congruent to triangle EFD.

Case (c): there is a right angle, so check the right angle, hypotenuse, side rule. The right angles are at B and D. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so it is AC in one triangle and FE in the other, and they are equal. A leg is equal too, AB = DF. The statement is triangle ABC congruent to triangle FDE.

Case (d): two angles and a side, and the side AC is not between the two angles. The third angles are equal too, because the three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. The rule is angle angle side, and the statement is triangle ABC congruent to triangle DEF.

Case (e): two sides, AB and AC, and the angle at B. Sketch it and ask whether B is squeezed between AB and AC. It is not, because AB and AC both start at A. So the angle is not between the two sides, and no rule guarantees that the triangles are twins.

(c) Congruent, right angle hypotenuse side: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle FDE. (d) Congruent, angle angle side: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. (e) Not guaranteed: the given angle at B is not between AB and AC, so it is the side side angle arrangement.

item.question: Segments AD and BC cross at O. It is given that OB equals OC and OA equals OD. Show that AB is parallel to CD. Hint: AD is a transversal for these two lines. Are there any equal alternate angles?
steps_tex: $OA = OD$ and $OB = OC$ are given.
The angles at $O$, angle $AOB$ and angle $DOC$, are vertically opposite, so angle $AOB =$ angle $DOC$.
Two sides and the angle between them match, so triangle $AOB$ is congruent to triangle $DOC$ by side angle side.
Matching parts of twins are equal, so angle $OAB =$ angle $ODC$.
$AD$ is a transversal that crosses $AB$ and $CD$, and angle $OAB$ and angle $ODC$ are alternate angles on it.
Equal alternate angles mean the two lines are parallel, so $AB$ is parallel to $CD$.

Hence angle $OAB =$ angle $ODC$. These are alternate angles for the transversal $AD$ cutting $AB$ and $CD$. Equal alternate angles mean the lines are parallel, so $AB$ is parallel to $CD$.

item.question: ABCD is a square. Show that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC. Is triangle ABC also congruent to triangle CDA? Give more examples of triangles that match their twin in two ways, and one that matches in six ways.
steps_tex: $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$ because the sides of a square are equal, and $AC$ belongs to both triangles, so it is equal to itself.
Three sides match, so triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $ADC$.
Try A onto $C$, $B$ onto $D$ and $C$ onto $A$: $AB = CD$, $BC = DA$ and $CA = AC$ all hold, so triangle $ABC$ is also congruent to triangle $CDA$.
Any isosceles triangle matches its twin in two ways, because the two equal sides can be swapped over.
An equilateral triangle matches in six ways, because every pairing of the letters lands.
item.answer_tex: Yes to both statements: $ABC$ is congruent to $ADC$ and to $CDA$. An isosceles triangle matches in two ways, an equilateral triangle in six.

item.question: Find angle B and angle C if A is the centre of the circle and the angle at A is 120 degrees.
steps_tex: $A$ is the centre, so $AB$ and $AC$ are both radii and $AB = AC$: the triangle is isosceles.
The three angles add to $180$ degrees, so angle $B +$ angle $C = 180 - 120 = 60$.
The two angles are equal, so each one is $60$ / $2 = 30$ degrees.

item.question: What are the main ideas of the chapter, in order?
item.answer: Congruent figures land exactly on each other, and turning or flipping is allowed. Triangles are congruent by side side side, side angle side, angle side angle, angle angle side or right angle, hypotenuse, side. Angle angle angle and side side angle do not guarantee it. Matching parts of congruent triangles are equal. Angles opposite equal sides are equal, and each angle of an equilateral triangle is sixty degrees.
item.text:

Matching parts of congruent triangles are equal. Angles opposite equal sides are equal, and each angle of an equilateral triangle is sixty degrees.

item.question: Draw lines to split the 24 white squares of the five by five grid, with the middle square left out, into 6 smaller regions that are all congruent.
steps: Count what is in play first: 25 squares less the blocked middle one leaves 24.
Six congruent pieces must be the same size, so each gets 24 / 6 = 4 squares.
Turning and flipping a piece is allowed, so each piece can lie any way up.
Lay a tracing of one piece over each other piece, turning or flipping it, to confirm that all six land.
item.answer: Six pieces of four squares each. Size first: 24 / 6 = 4 squares in every piece. Other layouts may also work.
